extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of history of mathematics and natural philosophy; general readers interested in evaluating historical scientific claims and eccentric works
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply criteria for judging historical mathematical/astronomical/technical claims and speculative works (e.g., quadratures, planetary habitation, constructed languages, alchemy) as discussed in a literary-historical essay. Focus is on epistemic standards, evidence, and practicability invoked by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification for arithmetic manipulations of ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: He had no right to presume that this mean was better than either of the extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating numerical approximations formed by combining numerators and denominators (e.g. taking the mean of two fractions by averaging numerators and denominators), require explicit justification or proof that the operation improves accuracy; the mere arithmetic mean of numerators/denominators is not a legitimate reason to claim superiority over given bounds. Anti-pattern: accepting such 'guesses' because they are convenient or produce close values without theoretical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish acknowledged fiction from asserted fact
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a class of hypothetical creations which do not belong to my subject, because they are acknowledged to be fictions ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before critiquing or treating a work as a claim about the world, establish whether the author acknowledges it as fiction. Treat acknowledged fictions (e.g. Lucian, Rabelais, Swift) as imaginative literature rather than factual or scientific assertions. Anti-pattern: criticizing imaginative works as if they advanced genuine empirical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anthropocentric and limited-analogy assumptions about extraterrestrial life
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole dispute tacitly assumes that, if the stars and planets be inhabited, it must be by things of which we can form some idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning about possible inhabitants or natures of other worlds, avoid assuming they must be forms we can readily conceive; explicitly acknowledge the limits of analogy. Consider that planetary matter and chemistry may be fundamentally different (e.g. 'There may be no oxygen and hydrogen in Jupiter'). Anti-pattern: treating terrestrial biology or chemistry as universal without argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate errors of demonstration from factual/opinion disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: My work selects, for the most part, sins against demonstration: but the world is full of questions of fact or opinion ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify mistakes into logical/methodological failures ('sins against demonstration') versus factual disagreements or contestable opinions. Use different standards of remedy: logical errors require refutation of method/proof, while factual/opinion disputes hinge on evidence and may change over time. Scoring note: give greater weight to failures of demonstration when assessing the reliability of intellectual work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicability and adoptability as criteria for constructed languages/systems
rubrics_metrics.description: One man may construct such a system--Bishop Wilkins has done it--but where is the man who will learn it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing proposals for constructed languages or universal notation systems, evaluate not just internal coherence but learnability and likelihood of adoption by others. A logically elegant system that nobody can or will learn is of limited practical value. Anti-pattern: valuing only theoretical completeness without regard to sociolinguistic feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contemporary documentary evidence for authorship attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: It is enough for me that Graunt ... was elected into the Royal Society because he was the author; that Petty refers to him as author in scores of places, and published an edition, as editor, after Graunt's death, with Graunt's name of course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute authorship on the basis of contemporaneous documentary indicators (elections, references by peers, editions published during/after life, editorial statements) rather than rumor or later conjecture. Anti-pattern: relying solely on hearsay or hostile accounts without checking primary records (e.g., company books, editions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand subject-matter competence of writers
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is unlearned who, be his other knowledge what it may, does not understand the subject he writes about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the credibility of an author's technical claims by whether the author demonstrably understands the relevant discipline. Treat confident but uninformed technical assertions skeptically. Anti-pattern: accepting grand claims from prominent literary figures or authorities outside the field without verifying technical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish arithmetical versus geometrical formulations of classical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The regular circle-squarers attempt the arithmetical quadrature, which has long been proved to be impossible. Very few attempt the geometrical quadrature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing purported solutions to classical problems (e.g., squaring the circle), first clarify whether the proposer aims at an arithmetical (numeric/analytic) or geometrical (construction) solution, since impossibility results and standards differ. Anti-pattern: conflating different flavors of a problem and misapplying impossibility proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require primary-source verification for historical claims about reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more incorrect [than saying men like Copernicus were universally derided] ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept broad historical generalizations (e.g., 'X was universally despised') without checking primary sources; historians should verify the range of contemporary responses rather than repeating simplified narratives. Anti-pattern: relying on later retellings or anecdotes without archival corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of prestige or office as substitute for genuine expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: This is the algebra of the Royal Household ... Quære, is it possible that the fame of Vieta ... could have given people the notion that when such an officer chose to declare himself an algebraist, he must be one indeed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate court/household rank or official titles with mathematical competence; evaluate the actual content and methods. Anti-pattern: granting credibility to mathematical claims because of the author's social position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize extraordinary technical claims and require rigorous refutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Longomontanus ... squared the circle in 1644 ... Among them, of course, Longomontanus was made mincemeat: but he is said to have insisted on the discovery of his epitaph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims of resolving famous impossibility problems with strong skepticism and demand detailed, rigorous demonstration; expect and value published refutations by competent mathematicians. Anti-pattern: uncritically repeating numerical approximations or 'solutions' without referencing community critique and refutation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss speculative pursuits solely because they seem currently improbable
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems, then, that the conviction that alchemy must be impossible was a delusion: but we do not mention it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain epistemic humility about long-term possibilities; while demanding evidence, avoid dogmatic dismissal of avenues that later science could vindicate (e.g., some aspects of alchemy becoming plausible in light of chemical discoveries). Scoring note: weigh historical context and evolving knowledge when judging past speculative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer documented publication for persistence and credit
rubrics_metrics.description: He published nothing; but his son Adrian ... first made it known in the work above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that unpublished or privately circulated work is more likely to be lost or misattributed; for establishing priority and credit, documented publication and dissemination matter. Anti-pattern: inferring priority from hearsay where no printed record exists.
